props.title: Try and Get Me

sections.content: Try and Get Me (1950), also known as "The Sound of Fury," stands as one of film noir's most brutal examinations of mob violence and social responsibility. Director Cy Endfield crafts a devastating critique of media sensationalism and crowd psychology, drawing clear parallels to the real-life 1933 San Jose lynching case. The film follows Frank Lovejoy as Howard Tyler, an unemployed family man who gets pulled into a criminal partnership with Lloyd Bridges' charismatic but psychopathic Jerry Slocum. Like The Ox-Bow Incident (1943) and Fury (1936), it powerfully depicts how ordinary citizens can transform into a murderous mob. movies.title: Try and Get Me
movies.slug: A desperate unemployed man falls in with a criminal, leading to tragedy and mob violence

sections.content: The film's unflinching portrayal of economic desperation resonates with other noir classics like Thieves' Highway (1949) and The Asphalt Jungle (1950), where financial pressure drives ordinary men to crime. But Endfield goes further, creating a damning portrait of how yellow journalism and public bloodlust can escalate violence. The climactic mob scene remains one of noir's most shocking sequences, rivaling the intensity of White Heat (1949) while carrying deeper social commentary.

What sets Try and Get Me apart is its raw psychological realism. Unlike more stylized noirs like Double Indemnity (1944) or Out of the Past (1947), Endfield opts for a documentary-like approach that heightens the horror. The film's examination of how media coverage can inflame public passions feels remarkably prescient, anticipating later works like Ace in the Hole (1951) and Network (1976). sections.content: The film exemplifies noir's capacity for social criticism, joining ranks with Force of Evil (1948) and The Phenix City Story (1955) in exposing systemic corruption and societal failures. Endfield's background in leftist theater influences the film's sharp critique of capitalism and mass media, though these elements led to his later blacklisting during the McCarthy era, similar to the fate of Salt of the Earth (1954) director Herbert Biberman.
